findings.quote: Coming soon — confirmed-safe snacks from CU, GS25, 7-Eleven, and Emart24, with package photos and flavor warnings.
findings.why: "Confirmed-safe" is an absolute guarantee. Nothing established by reading a Korean package can confirm safety for celiac disease: mandatory allergen labelling covers wheat only, barley and rye are not mandatory, and shared-line cross-contamination is never disclosed on-label. This sets a reader expectation that the eventual post cannot honour.
findings.fix: Replace with a claim the method can support, e.g. "snacks whose labels list no wheat, with the limits of Korean labelling explained". Reserve "safe" for products with manufacturer confirmation or third-party GF certification, and say which is which.

findings.quote: The "flip-and-scan" routine — 4 steps for any package
findings.why: A package-scanning routine is presented as the engine that yields "confirmed gluten-free" results. That is the method-versus-claim gap: label scanning establishes what is declared, not what is present. The page states no limits at all.
findings.fix: State the method plainly and bound it: what scanning a label can show (declared wheat), what it cannot (barley, rye, malt, soy sauce derivatives, shared equipment), and what additional step — manufacturer contact or certification — was used for any product called safe.

findings.quote: 12+ confirmed gluten-free snacks with package photos
findings.why: The page's load-bearing claim is stated as settled fact with zero supporting detail — no products, no ingredient text, no source, no check date. A reader has only the author's word for a safety-relevant assertion.
findings.fix: Either remove the count and the word "confirmed" until the list is published, or publish the list with per-product ingredient text, the date each label was read, and the store and region where it was bought.

findings.why: The title asserts current-year authority for a page dated 4 May 2026 that is still empty on 12 August 2026, and no check dates are attached to any claim. Korean manufacturers reformulate silently, so an undated snack list ages into a hazard.
findings.fix: Add a visible "last verified" date to every product entry when published, and add a standing note that formulations change and readers must re-read the label at purchase.

findings.quote: Email **contact@noglutenkorea.com** or follow **[@noglutenkorea](https://instagram.com/noglutenkorea)** to know when this lands.
findings.why: The only reader action offered is subscribing. There is no Korean ingredient vocabulary, no photograph of a label, and no manufacturer contact route, so the reader cannot independently check any safety claim the page makes.
findings.fix: Give the reader the Korean terms to look for (밀, 소맥분, 보리, 맥아, 호밀, 간장) plus manufacturer customer-service contact details, so verification does not depend on trusting the author.

findings.quote: Flavor-specific warnings (NOT all flavors of one brand are safe)
findings.why: The flavour-variation point is correct and useful, but it is framed as a brand quirk rather than as a consequence of Korean labelling and seasoning practice, and the page never states the load-bearing fact that only wheat is a mandatory allergen declaration.
findings.fix: Anchor the warning in the labelling regime: explain that wheat must be declared but barley, rye and malt need not be, which is why flavour seasonings differ in risk within one brand.
